title: Moving to Costa Rica: A Buyer's Guide to Actually Making the Move
excerpt: The move in the order that actually works: pick the town before the house, rent through a green season, match your title to your residency plan, and know the real carrying costs before you buy.
meta_desc: A step-by-step guide to moving to Costa Rica: choosing your town, renting first, residency paths, real carrying costs, schools, and buying the right property.
body:
**If you are thinking about moving to Costa Rica, or buying property here so you can move later, message me and I will help you think it through.** I am Tiago Leao, an agent with KRAIN on the Guanacaste Gold Coast, and my own family made this exact move 15 years ago. You do not need to be ready to buy, ready to move, or ready to do anything except ask a question. [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) is the fastest way to reach me and I answer every message myself, in English, Spanish or Portuguese.

The rest of this guide is what I would tell you on that call, written down.

Moving to Costa Rica is really two decisions that people usually collapse into one: where you want your life to be, and what you want to own. Almost everything that goes wrong in a relocation comes from doing the second one before the first. So this walks the move in the order that actually works, from your first exploratory trip to the day you get the keys, with the costs, the timelines, and the mistakes I watch buyers make from the inside.

I grew up in these beach towns and went through the residency process myself as a dependent. Today I spend my days with American and Canadian families doing what my family did, and I have watched enough of these moves land well, and a few land badly, to know where the difference comes from.

## Start by naming what kind of move this is

There are really only three versions of moving to Costa Rica, and each one points at a different property.

**The full-time move.** You are selling or renting out the house back home and living here. Your priorities are the boring ones: water supply, internet reliability, drive time to a good hospital, drive time to school, whether the road floods in October. Ocean view matters less than you think it will after month four.

**The part-time move.** You are here three to six months a year, usually escaping winter, and the house earns when you are not in it. Now rental performance, management, and location convenience become real financial variables. Start with [what vacation rental income actually looks like in Guanacaste](/blog/costa-rica-vacation-rental-income-guanacaste/), because the gap between gross and net surprises almost everyone.

**The investment-first move.** You buy now, rent it out, and move later. This is the most flexible path and it has a genuine advantage: your property can double as your residency qualification if you structure it right from day one.

Say which one you are out loud before you look at a single listing. The answer changes the town, the price band, the property type, and how you take title.

## Choose the region before the house

Costa Rica is small on a map and large in practice. The Caribbean side, the Central Valley, the Southern Zone, and Guanacaste are four different countries as far as your daily life is concerned. I work Guanacaste, so I will be straight about what that means: dry, sunny, beach-town living with a real dry season and a green season, the country's second international airport at Liberia, and the highest concentration of North American families on the coast.

Inside Guanacaste, the towns are not interchangeable either. Tamarindo is the town with everything, restaurants, schools, services, and the noise that comes with them. Playa Grande is quiet, surf-driven, protected. Flamingo, Potrero and Brasilito are the marina and residential corridor. Conchal is resort-anchored and manicured. Nosara is further out, wellness-focused, and a genuinely different drive.

The single most useful thing you can do here is read a comparison rather than a brochure:

- [Guanacaste's beach towns, compared](/blog/guanacaste-gold-coast-towns-guide/)
- [Tamarindo vs. Playa Grande](/blog/tamarindo-vs-playa-grande-real-estate/)
- [Flamingo vs. Conchal vs. Potrero](/blog/flamingo-vs-conchal-vs-potrero-real-estate/)
- [Tamarindo vs. Nosara](/blog/tamarindo-vs-nosara-real-estate/)

Or skip the reading and just ask me. Send me a message on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) with who is moving, roughly what the budget is, and whether there are kids, and I will tell you which two or three of these towns to spend your first trip in and which ones to skip. That is a fifteen-minute conversation and it has saved people entire trips.

## Rent first. Costa Rica gives you 180 days to be sure

Americans and Canadians can enter as tourists and stay up to 180 days. That is half a year to live somewhere before you commit, and very few countries hand you that much runway.

Use it deliberately. Rent in two towns, not one. Be here in September or October, when the green season is at its wettest, not only in February when everything is postcard-perfect. Drive the school run at 7am. Sit in your prospective neighborhood at 9pm on a Saturday and listen. Get the internet speed test at the actual house.

Most of my best client relationships start a year or more before a purchase, with exactly this. I would rather help you rent, and be the person you call fourteen months later, than sell you the wrong house in week two.

## The money picture: what living here actually costs

Two categories, and people usually get the first one right and the second one wrong.

**Cost of living** is genuinely lower than most of the US and Canada in the places that matter: healthcare, property taxes, help around the house, produce, eating locally. It is not lower in the places people forget: imported groceries, cars, electronics, appliances, air conditioning in April, private school tuition, and anything that arrives in a shipping container. Beach-town Guanacaste is also the most expensive part of Costa Rica. Budgets built from a blog post about Atenas or Grecia do not survive contact with Tamarindo.

**Carrying costs on the property** are the part I can be precise about, because they are structural:

- **Property tax: 0.25 percent** of registered value per year. On a $600,000 home that is $1,500. The [full property tax breakdown](/blog/costa-rica-property-taxes-explained/), including the Luxury Home Tax that applies to higher-value homes, is here.
- **HOA and community fees** vary enormously and are the real number to interrogate, especially in gated and resort communities where they can dwarf the tax bill.
- **Insurance, pool and garden service, pest control, and maintenance.** Salt air, humidity and sun are hard on a house. Deferred maintenance here compounds faster than it does in a temperate climate.
- **Closing costs: roughly 3.5 to 4.5 percent** of the purchase price, one time, usually paid by the buyer. See the [closing costs and taxes guide](/blog/costa-rica-closing-costs-taxes/).

If you want the honest carrying-cost math on a specific property rather than a general range, send me the listing on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660), whether it is one of mine or not, and I will build the real number with you line by line. That exercise alone has changed which house a few of my clients bought.

## Residency: pick your lane early

You do not need residency to buy property here. Foreigners own titled property outright, in their own name, with the same rights as citizens. But if you are moving, you will want residency eventually, and the category you qualify for should influence how you buy.

- **Pensionado** requires $1,000 a month in lifetime pension income. Social Security and CPP qualify; 401(k) withdrawals do not.
- **Rentista** requires $2,500 a month in guaranteed unearned income, or the cleaner route, a $60,000 deposit in a Costa Rican bank.
- **Inversionista** requires a $150,000 investment, and real estate counts. This is the path most of my clients take, because the purchase they already wanted to make does double duty.

The detail that costs people money: for Inversionista, the property generally needs to be registered in your **personal name**, not a corporation. Corporations are common here for other good reasons. If you decide on the structure after closing, you may be paying to fix it. Tell your attorney your residency plan at the start, not at signing.

The full breakdown, including CAJA, timelines and taxes, is in my [residency guide for property buyers](/blog/costa-rica-residency-property-buyers/).

## Healthcare, honestly

Residents enroll in CAJA, the public system, at roughly 9 to 11 percent of declared income, and it covers a spouse and children under 18 at no extra cost. Most expats I know use CAJA as their backbone and pay out of pocket or carry private insurance for speed and choice, because private care here costs a fraction of US prices.

The relocation-specific question is not "is healthcare good," it is "how far am I from it." In Guanacaste, routine care is local, the regional hospital is in Liberia, and the top private hospitals are in San José. For most families that is fine. If someone in your household has a condition that needs frequent specialist care, drive time to San José belongs in your town decision, not as an afterthought.

## Families: solve school before you solve house

This is the one I feel strongest about. If you have school-age kids, the school decision constrains the house decision, not the other way around. Guanacaste has a real cluster of bilingual and international schools, but seats are finite, calendars differ, and admissions can run months ahead. Families who fall in love with a house 45 minutes from the school they end up choosing regret it every single morning.

Start with my [guide to schools on the Guanacaste Gold Coast](/blog/schools-guanacaste-gold-coast-guide/) and the [school profiles](/schools.html), then draw your search radius around the school. If you tell me your kids' ages I can tell you which schools are realistically taking students this year, which is not always what the websites say.

## The logistics nobody puts in the brochure

- **Shipping a container.** Common, taxable, and slower than quoted. Many people ship the sentimental and buy the rest here. Furniture that thrives in humidity is not the furniture in your living room right now.
- **Cars.** Import duties are high and used-car prices reflect it. A vehicle that is unremarkable in Denver is expensive here. Budget accordingly, and buy something with clearance if you are outside a paved development.
- **Pets.** Very doable, with health certificates and airline-specific rules. Start earlier than you think; summer heat embargoes catch people out.
- **Banking.** Opening a local account as a non-resident is possible but paperwork-heavy, and it gets much easier once you have a DIMEX. Most buyers close in dollars through escrow long before they have a local account.
- **Internet.** Fiber has reached most of the developed coast and is genuinely good where it exists. "Most" is doing work in that sentence. If you work remotely, test the speed at the specific house, and ask what the backup is.
- **Driving.** Your foreign license works while your tourist entry is valid. Waze is standard, addresses are descriptive rather than numeric, and one river crossing in October will teach you more about your route than any map.

## Then, and only then, buy the property

Once you know the town, the school, and your residency lane, the purchase itself is refreshingly orderly. Costa Rica has a centralized national registry, closings run through a notary attorney, and funds move through a regulated escrow company.

The sequence:

1. **Offer and negotiation.** Your agent presents and negotiates terms.
2. **Purchase and sale agreement**, with a deposit, commonly around 10 percent, into [escrow](/blog/costa-rica-real-estate-escrow-guide/).
3. **Due diligence**, typically 15 to 30 days. Your attorney examines title and liens, the survey plan, the [water letter](/blog/costa-rica-property-water-letter-guide/), permits and use-of-land. My [due-diligence checklist](/blog/costa-rica-property-due-diligence-checklist/) is what I hand clients.
4. **Closing.** The deed is signed before a notary and recorded in the registry.

Two Costa Rica-specific things to internalize before you shop. First, most transactions are cash, because local financing for foreigners is limited and expensive; many buyers use home equity or a securities-backed line from home when they want leverage. Second, beachfront is not what it looks like: the first 200 meters from the high tide line is the maritime zone, and most of it is concession land rather than title. Read [titled vs. concession beachfront](/blog/titled-vs-concession-beachfront-costa-rica/) before you fall for anything on the sand.

If you are considering building instead of buying, the real constraints are water availability, the permit chain and construction timelines, not the land price. Start with [what it costs to build in Guanacaste](/blog/cost-to-build-house-guanacaste-costa-rica/) and the [land buying checklist](/blog/buying-land-guanacaste-zoning-water-building-checklist/).

## What actually surprises people in year one

Not the bugs, not the Spanish, not the roads. It is these:

- **Everything takes longer.** Permits, deliveries, repairs, bureaucracy. The people who thrive here stop treating this as a problem to solve and start treating it as the price of admission.
- **The green season is real.** May through November, with September and October the heaviest. It is green, lush and quiet, and it is also when things leak and roads wash. Owning here means budgeting for it.
- **Maintenance is not optional.** A house on this coast needs a person who watches it. If you are part-time, property management is a line item, not a luxury.
- **Community is the whole thing.** The families who stay are the ones who joined something in the first six months, the surf group, the school, the volunteer thing, the Tuesday soccer game. The ones who leave are usually the ones who bought a beautiful house and waited for a life to show up.

## A realistic 18-month timeline

1. **Months 1 to 3.** Exploratory trip. Two towns minimum. Meet an agent and an immigration attorney, ask hard questions, buy nothing.
2. **Months 3 to 6.** Choose your residency category. Start gathering and apostilling documents at home, they are typically only valid for six months, so sequence them.
3. **Months 4 to 9.** Rent here for a stretch, ideally including part of the green season. If you have kids, apply to schools now.
4. **Months 6 to 12.** Shop seriously in one or two towns. Offer, escrow, due diligence, close. Structure title to match your residency plan.
5. **Months 9 to 15.** File the residency application. You can remain in the country legally while it processes once filed.
6. **Months 12 to 18.** Move in, ship or buy, enroll in CAJA, get your DIMEX, and start the part that no checklist covers.

Some people compress this to six months. Some take five years. Both are fine. The order is what matters.

## Let's talk about your move

Most of my clients start talking to me long before they are ready to buy, and that is exactly how it should work. The useful conversations happen while you are still deciding, not after you have already fallen for a house.

I grew up here. I went through this process from the inside, with my own family, at an age where I watched every part of it. I live on this coast full time, I work in **English, Spanish and Portuguese**, and I represent buyers across the Gold Coast with KRAIN, from Tamarindo through Playa Grande, Flamingo, Brasilito and Conchal.

What you get by reaching out, none of which costs anything and none of which requires you to be a client:

- **A straight answer about which towns fit you.** Not a list of all of them. Two or three, and the reasons, and which ones to skip.
- **The people, not just the properties.** Immigration attorneys, closing attorneys, escrow companies, inspectors, builders, property managers, school contacts. My clients tell me the vetted list is worth more than any listing.
- **Honest carrying-cost math** on any property you are considering, mine or someone else's, including the HOA fee that most listings gloss over.
- **A read on timing.** Whether what you want exists at your number right now, or whether you should wait, rent, or widen the search.
- **Me telling you not to buy something.** Regularly. I would rather lose a transaction than sell a family a house 45 minutes from their school or a beachfront lot that turns out to be concession rather than title.

### The easiest way to start

Send me a WhatsApp message with these four things. It takes a minute to write and it is enough for me to give you something genuinely useful back:

1. **Who is moving** and roughly when.
2. **Your budget range**, even a wide one.
3. **Kids, and their ages**, if any.
4. **What you would be doing here**: retiring, working remotely, renting the place out, or still figuring that out.

I answer every message myself. Not an assistant, not a form, not a drip campaign.

**[Message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).** You can also find me on [Instagram](https://instagram.com/soldbytiago) or email tiago@soldbytiago.com.

If you are somewhere between "we talk about this on Sunday nights" and "we fly down next month," that is the right time to reach out. And if you would rather read a while longer first, my [Buyer's Guide](/buyers-guide.html) covers the transaction mechanics and [current listings](/properties.html) will calibrate your budget faster than any price article.

*This article is general information, not legal, tax or immigration advice. Immigration categories, tax thresholds and municipal practice change, and every situation differs. Confirm current requirements with a licensed Costa Rican immigration attorney, real estate attorney and accountant before acting. References: [Direccion General de Migracion](https://www.migracion.go.cr), [Ministerio de Hacienda](https://www.hacienda.go.cr), [CCSS](https://www.ccss.sa.cr), [Registro Nacional](https://www.registronacional.go.cr). Cost-of-living observations reflect the Guanacaste coast in 2026 and are my own, not survey data.*

## FAQ

### How much money do you need to move to Costa Rica?

It depends on the residency path and the lifestyle. The formal minimums are $1,000 a month in lifetime pension income for Pensionado, $2,500 a month in unearned income or a $60,000 bank deposit for Rentista, and a $150,000 investment for Inversionista. Beach-town Guanacaste costs meaningfully more to live in than the Central Valley, so budgets built from national averages tend to run short.

### Can I move to Costa Rica without residency?

You can live here on tourist entries of up to 180 days and buy property with full ownership rights, since foreigners have the same property rights as citizens. What you cannot do without residency is enroll in CAJA, work for a Costa Rican company, or stay indefinitely without leaving. Most people who move permanently start on a tourist entry and file for residency within the first year.

### Should I rent or buy first when moving to Costa Rica?

Rent first, almost always. The 180-day tourist entry gives you enough time to live in two towns, experience the green season, and test the school run before committing. The most expensive mistakes I see come from buying in week two of a first visit.

### Is Guanacaste a good place to move with kids?

It is one of the easier parts of Costa Rica for families, because the Gold Coast has a cluster of bilingual and international schools and a large established North American community. The practical rule is to choose the school first and then search for a house inside a sane drive of it, since seats are limited and commutes here are longer than the distance suggests.

### What is the biggest mistake people make moving to Costa Rica?

Buying before they have lived here through a green season, and buying without matching the title structure to their residency plan. The first produces a house in the wrong town; the second produces legal work you pay for twice.

## About the author

Tiago Leao is a real estate agent with KRAIN Luxury Real Estate on the Guanacaste Gold Coast, working Tamarindo, Playa Grande, Flamingo, Brasilito and Conchal. His family moved to Costa Rica 15 years ago and he went through the residency process himself, which is why relocating buyers make up most of his business. He works in English, Spanish and Portuguese, and builds every signature listing its own dedicated marketing page at [soldbytiago.com/signature/](https://soldbytiago.com/signature/). Reach him on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).

title: Best Places to Live in Costa Rica With Kids: The 2026 Family Guide
excerpt: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, Flamingo and Potrero, and Tamarindo: where families actually settle on the Guanacaste coast, which schools each one is close to, and what to know before you move.
meta_desc: The best areas to live in Costa Rica with kids in 2026: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, Flamingo, Potrero and Tamarindo, with nearby international schools and a family moving checklist.
body:
**If you are moving to Costa Rica with kids, the best areas to live in 2026 are Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, and Flamingo and Potrero, with Tamarindo as the pick for families who want to walk to everything.** Each one sits close to at least one established international school, and that single fact matters more than the house, the view, or the price.

I am Tiago Leao, a real estate agent with KRAIN on the Guanacaste Gold Coast. My family moved to Costa Rica 15 years ago, I grew up on these beaches, and I graduated from CRIA, one of the schools in this guide, five years ago. So when parents ask me where to live, I am answering as someone who did the school run here, not just someone who sells houses here.

If you came here from my video, this is the full guide I promised. If you want help with your specific family, [message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) with your kids' ages and I will tell you where I would look.

## Start with the school, not the house

Every family I work with asks about the house first. Within a week, they are asking about the school first. Here is why, and it is the most important thing in this entire guide:

**The school decides the town. The town decides the commute. The commute decides which houses are even worth seeing.**

A few things that surprise almost every parent:

- **There are no school ratings here.** No GreatSchools, no state test scores, no independent body ranking schools on a comparable scale. Anyone showing you a score for a Costa Rican school made it up. The visit is the research.
- **Assume there is no school bus.** Some schools run transport and some do not. Plan on driving twice a day until a school tells you otherwise in writing.
- **The good schools have waitlists.** Grades 6 through 9 are the tightest. Families who arrive in July expecting to sort school out in August can find nothing available until the following February.
- **A school 12 km away is not 12 minutes away.** Roads bend around rivers and hills, and in the rainy months some of them get slow. Drive the route at 7am on a weekday before you buy.

The full breakdown of every school on this coast, with curriculum, grades and accreditation, is in my [guide to schools in Guanacaste](/blog/schools-guanacaste-gold-coast-guide/). You can also browse [every school profile](/schools.html) on my site.

## 1. Hacienda Pinilla

Hacienda Pinilla is where I sell more homes than anywhere else on this coast, and families are a big reason why.

It is a large gated beach and golf community on the coast just south of Tamarindo. According to the resort's own published materials, it includes:

- **Gated, controlled access**, which is the first thing most relocating parents ask about
- **Multiple beaches**, including Playa Avellanas, one of Guanacaste's best-known surf breaks, plus Mansita and Bonita inside the resort
- **A beachfront Beach Club**
- **An 18-hole golf course**, tennis and pickleball
- **Mountain bike and hiking trails** through tropical dry forest
- **An equestrian center**
- **Tons of open space**, which is the part kids actually care about

**For school:** Pinilla sits close to Tamarindo, which puts you within reach of [TIDE Academy](/school/tide-academy/), a small school of around 80 students from 17 countries with an 8:1 student-teacher ratio, and [Journey School](/school/journey-school-tamarindo/), an IB World School running Pre-K through 12. It is a drive rather than a walk, so test the route in the morning.

**Best for:** families who want space, security and an outdoor life, and do not mind driving into Tamarindo for school and errands.

**Keep in mind:** Pinilla is organized into separate neighborhoods, each with its own fees and rules. Two similar homes can carry very different monthly costs. Get the fee schedule for the specific section in writing.

More detail is in my [Hacienda Pinilla guide](/blog/hacienda-pinilla-communities-amenities-guide/) and on my [Hacienda Pinilla community page](/development/hacienda-pinilla/).

## 2. Reserva Conchal

Reserva Conchal is the most complete master-planned community on this coast, and it is the one with the strongest school story of all.

It rises behind Playa Conchal, the crushed-shell beach between Brasilito and Flamingo. Per the resort's published materials, you get:

- **A private gated community** with controlled access
- **The beach**, with a private Beach Club right on Playa Conchal
- **A championship golf course**
- **Trails and restaurants**, plus the Westin and the W operating inside the gates
- **Seventeen residential communities**, from condos and townhomes to custom homes and lots

**For school:** [Costa Rica International Academy (CRIA)](/school/costa-rica-international-academy/) is basically right outside, about 500 meters from the entrance. It is U.S.-accredited and bilingual, sits on a 32-acre campus, and has been running since 2000, which makes it one of the longest-established international schools on the coast.

I graduated from CRIA five years ago and had a great experience there. I am not a neutral observer on this one, and I will not pretend to be.

**Best for:** families who want amenities managed for them, a U.S.-track education, and the shortest school run on this list.

**Keep in mind:** living inside a working resort, with hotels inside the gates, is exactly the appeal for some families and a deal-breaker for others. Each of the seventeen communities also has its own fees, so compare them carefully.

More in my [Reserva Conchal guide](/blog/reserva-conchal-real-estate-communities-guide/) and on my [Reserva Conchal community page](/development/reserva-conchal/).

## 3. Flamingo and Potrero

If Pinilla and Conchal are resort living, Flamingo and Potrero are a real beach town. For a lot of families, that is the whole point.

You get a quieter beach-town lifestyle, the Flamingo Marina, restaurants, grocery stores, and a year-round community that keeps growing. The two towns sit next to each other and feel different:

- **Flamingo** has the white-sand showpiece beach, the marina, and hillside homes with big ocean views.
- **Potrero** wraps a calm, protected bay. The water is the swimmable, paddleable kind, which matters a lot more than people expect when your kids are small. It is also where your money goes furthest on this stretch of coast.

### Mar Vista, the one to know about

Tucked on the hillside between Brasilito and Flamingo is **Mar Vista**, a master-planned community built around a clubhouse with an infinity pool, the Gracia restaurant, tennis and pickleball courts, and hiking and biking trails.

Here is why families should know the name: [La Paz Community School's Cabo Velas campus](/school/la-paz-community-school-cabo-velas/) sits right at Mar Vista's entrance. That makes it the only large community on this coast with an accredited international school at its gate. La Paz is an IB World School, PreK through 12, with dual-language immersion.

If a walkable or near-walkable school run is your dream, this is about as close as it gets here. More in my [Mar Vista guide](/blog/mar-vista-flamingo-real-estate-guide/) and on my [Mar Vista community page](/development/mar-vista/).

**For school:** La Paz is very close to Flamingo and Potrero, and CRIA is a short drive south by Conchal. Having two strong, different schools nearby gives you a real choice, which not every area can offer.

**Best for:** families who want a genuine town instead of a gated resort, calm water for little kids, and a community of people who actually live here year-round.

**Keep in mind:** Flamingo's hills mean driving to the beach and dinner. Potrero has fewer amenities than the resort communities today.

For the side-by-side comparison, read [Flamingo vs Conchal vs Potrero](/blog/flamingo-vs-conchal-vs-potrero-real-estate/), and see my [Flamingo](/flamingo.html) and [Potrero](/potrero.html) town pages.

## Bonus: Tamarindo, if you want to walk to everything

Tamarindo did not make my top three for one reason: it is busy. But for some families that energy is exactly right, so it belongs in this guide.

It is the most developed town on the coast. Restaurants, surf schools, shops and services are all close together, and in parts of town you really can walk to the beach and to dinner. It also has the most school options in one place:

- [Journey School](/school/journey-school-tamarindo/), IB World School, Pre-K through 12
- [TIDE Academy](/school/tide-academy/), small, personalized, and deliberately different
- [Educarte](/school/educarte/), bilingual and MEP-certified out toward Huacas, and the only school on this coast that publishes its tuition

Newer communities on the hillside, like [Tamarindo Park](/blog/tamarindo-park-real-estate-buyers-guide/) and [Senderos](/blog/senderos-tamarindo-real-estate-guide/), give you more space while staying close to town.

**Best for:** families with teenagers who want independence, parents who hate driving, and anyone who wants a lively town.

**Keep in mind:** the same energy that makes Tamarindo fun makes it louder and busier, especially in high season. More on the [Tamarindo town page](/tamarindo.html).

## Which area fits your family?

- **You want space, security and nature:** Hacienda Pinilla
- **You want a U.S.-accredited school minutes away and everything managed for you:** Reserva Conchal
- **You want an IB school at your gate:** Mar Vista in Flamingo
- **You want a real town and calm water for small kids:** Potrero
- **You want to walk to things and have the most school choices:** Tamarindo

## What else to know before you move

### Choosing a curriculum

If there is any chance your kids will finish school somewhere else, **IB travels best.** On this stretch of coast that means Journey and La Paz. If you want a U.S.-track education, CRIA is the anchor. If there is any chance your kids stay in the Costa Rican system, ask every school directly about **MEP accreditation**, which is what makes a diploma valid here.

### Healthcare for the kids

If you get residency, you enroll in CAJA, the public healthcare system. Once the primary applicant is enrolled, **a spouse and children under 18 are covered at no additional cost.** Many families also carry private insurance or pay out of pocket at private clinics for speed and choice.

### Residency covers the whole family

You do not need a separate application for every child. **One qualifying applicant can include a spouse and dependent children.** I went through residency myself as a dependent when my family moved here. The full breakdown of the three main paths is in my [residency guide](/blog/costa-rica-residency-property-buyers/).

### Rent before you buy

Americans and Canadians can stay up to 180 days on a tourist entry. Use that time. Rent in the area you are leaning toward, enroll the kids if you can, and live through a rainy season before you commit to a house. My [guide to moving to Costa Rica](/blog/moving-to-costa-rica-buyers-guide/) walks through the whole move in the order that actually works.

### A realistic order of operations

1. Pick two or three schools based on curriculum, not on the town you liked on vacation.
2. Call them and ask about openings in your kid's exact grade for your exact start date.
3. Visit every one in person.
4. Drive the route from the areas you are considering, at 7am on a weekday.
5. Then start looking at homes.

Families who do it in this order settle in. Families who buy the house first are often back on the market within two years.

## FAQ

### What is the best area in Costa Rica to live with kids?

On the Guanacaste Gold Coast, the strongest areas for families are Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, and Flamingo and Potrero, with Tamarindo for families who want walkability. The right one depends on which school you choose, because the school run shapes daily life more than any other factor.

### Are there good international schools in Guanacaste?

Yes. Established options include CRIA, a U.S.-accredited bilingual school next to Reserva Conchal; La Paz Community School, an IB World School at the entrance to Mar Vista in Flamingo; and Journey School and TIDE Academy in Tamarindo. There are no official school ratings in Costa Rica, so visiting in person is the real research.

### Is Hacienda Pinilla good for families?

For families who want space and security, yes. It is gated, has multiple beaches, a Beach Club, trails, golf, tennis and an equestrian center, and it is close to Tamarindo's schools including TIDE Academy and Journey School. School is a drive rather than a walk.

### Which school is near Reserva Conchal?

Costa Rica International Academy (CRIA) is about 500 meters from the Reserva Conchal entrance. It is U.S.-accredited and bilingual and has operated since 2000.

### Do kids get healthcare in Costa Rica?

Residents enroll in CAJA, Costa Rica's public healthcare system, and once the primary applicant is enrolled, a spouse and children under 18 are covered at no additional cost. Many families add private insurance as well.

### When should I start looking at schools before moving?

Before you choose a town, and ideally months ahead of your move. Waitlists are real, especially for grades 6 through 9, and families who wait until they arrive can find no openings until the following school term.
